summaries.gardner: IBM is the opposite of a Rule Breaker: a 115-year-old incumbent growing revenue 4-8% a year rather than the top dog of an emerging industry. Its quantum computing and Red Hat franchises add some forward-looking appeal, but the stock has lagged the market over the past year and is not widely called overvalued, so it fits Gardner's approach poorly.
summaries.buffett: IBM has durable switching costs in mainframes and core software, a 31-year record of dividend increases and strong free cash flow ($14.7B in 2025), which echo Buffett's tenets. However, Berkshire itself sold its IBM stake in 2017-2018 after earnings disappointed, return on capital leans on about $62B of debt, and per-share earnings are lower than a decade ago, so the fit is partial.
summaries.munger: Munger favoured simple, great businesses with wide moats at fair prices; IBM's mainframe lock-in is a genuine moat, but its sprawling mix of consulting, hardware, software and quantum is hard to judge as 'great'. Inverting the problem, AI-driven code migration and hyperscaler competition are real ways the moat could erode, so it is at best a fair business at a fair price.
summaries.lynch: IBM reads as a stalwart with a turnaround flavour: a well-known large company growing revenue mid-single digits with a 3% dividend yield. With a forward P/E near 18 against expected EPS growth of about 6-7%, its PEG is well above 1, so Lynch's valuation tests are not met even though the story is easy to understand.
summaries.fisher: IBM scores well on Fisher's R&D and product-development points ($8.3B of R&D in 2025, new Telum II and Spyre chips, Granite models and a quantum roadmap to 2029) and has a long-tenured management bench. It scores less well on sales growth potential and on its record of turning research into dominant products in recent decades.
summaries.graham: IBM passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and 20-year dividend tests, but fails on valuation and earnings growth: diluted EPS of $11.17 in 2025 is below $13.42 in 2015, the price is about 27 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B is well above 22.5. A defensive Graham investor would not buy at today's price.
summaries.thiel: IBM is not a zero-to-one company in most of its business; it competes in crowded consulting, cloud and AI markets without a 10x technology edge. Its mainframe niche and its quantum ambitions are closest to Thiel's ideal of monopoly-like positions, but neither currently drives growth.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for companies riding a major platform shift with improving growth and efficiency; IBM is a beneficiary of enterprise AI (generative AI book of business above $12.5B by January 2026) and has improved margins and free cash flow. Yet growth slowed to 1% in Q2 2026 and guidance was cut, so it does not look like a compounding AI leader he would concentrate in.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on accelerating earnings, rising estimates and positive catalysts with strong price trends; IBM's shares are down about 18% over 52 weeks, full-year growth guidance was trimmed in July 2026 and estimates are not rising sharply. Possible catalysts such as Confluent integration, the Lightwell security launch and the next mainframe cycle exist, but the setup does not fit his style.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith wants high-return, cash-generative businesses that do not need much debt; IBM has high gross margins (58.2% in 2025) and solid free cash flow but carries about $62B of debt, has a ROIC in the low teens and has delivered weak long-run revenue growth. It falls short of Fundsmith's 'good company' bar.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, IBM's earnings yield (EBIT of about $12.8B over an enterprise value of about $270B, roughly 4.7%) is low, and its return on capital is moderate. It would not rank near the top of a Greenblatt screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs an extraordinary business, talented and honest management, and high-return reinvestment; IBM has a decent business and capable, candid management, but limited ability to reinvest internally at high returns, relying instead on large debt-funded acquisitions such as HashiCorp and Confluent. It fits only partly.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple, distressed businesses with durable moats bought at large discounts (heads I win, tails I don't lose much); IBM's February 2026 sell-off on AI-coding fears gave a temporary setback, but at about 15-16 times free cash flow the price is not deeply discounted and the moat's durability is the open question. It is not a classic Dhandho bet.
summaries.wood: IBM is active in AI and quantum computing, two of ARK's innovation themes, but its revenue base is mostly legacy consulting, mainframes and software growing in single digits. ARK's approach favours fast-growing disruptors, and IBM is more often cast as an incumbent at risk of disruption.
summaries.ackman: Ackman looks for simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and strong balance sheets; IBM's recurring software and mainframe revenue is predictable and cash-generative, but its balance sheet is leveraged (about $62B of debt against $8B of cash) and its competitive position outside mainframes is not dominant. The fit is partial.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model rewards companies that pass scale benefits back to customers and grow stronger over time; IBM does not clearly do this, and its moat is defensive lock-in rather than an ever-widening cost advantage. It does not fit Nomad's ideal.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed companies attacking huge, fast-growing markets with technology that solves big, painful problems; IBM's quantum effort and AI-driven automation address large problems, but the company as a whole is a mature incumbent rather than a market-creating startup. It is not the kind of company his framework targets.
summaries.nash: IBM fails most of Nash's hard filters: revenue growth is below 10%, debt far exceeds cash, operating margin is below 20% and his 12% DCF gives a value well below the share price. It passes his zone-to-avoid and hype-trap tests, but scores about 70 on his 13-category scorecard, under the 75 bar.

momentum.evidence: IBM shares closed at $227.88 on October 14, 2026, down about 17.7% over 52 weeks, while the S&P 500 rose; the stock fell sharply in February 2026 on AI-coding fears and again after the July 2026 guidance cut.

g4.evidence: CEO Arvind Krishna has led a credible turnaround since 2020 and institutions own about 66% of the shares, but there is no well-known star investor backing it and Berkshire Hathaway exited in 2017-2018.

g6.evidence: Commentators mostly debate whether IBM is a value trap or a buy-the-dip opportunity after a roughly 20%+ drop from its 2026 high; few call it overvalued.

simple.evidence: The four segments (Software 44%, Consulting 31%, Infrastructure 23% and Financing 1% of 2025 revenue) are understandable, but judging the durability of mainframe lock-in and AI disruption risk requires specialist knowledge.

b2.evidence: IBM has been profitable and paid dividends for decades and grew revenue every year from 2020 to 2025, but revenue and EPS are still below their 2010s levels after decades of shrinkage and divestitures.

integrity.evidence: Management is candid (Krishna's July 14, 2026 letter openly said IBM 'did not adapt and move quickly enough'), but IBM relies heavily on non-GAAP 'operating' EPS ($11.59 vs $11.17 GAAP in 2025) and has made large debt-funded acquisitions.

b6.evidence: IBM has narrowed its focus (Kyndryl spin-off in 2021, sale of Watson Health in 2022), but it has also spent heavily on acquisitions, $8.3B in 2025 and about $10.5B in the first half of 2026.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 14% and ROE about 34%, but the ROE is inflated by leverage: total debt of $62.0B against equity of $34.5B at June 30, 2026.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $14.7B against GAAP net income of $10.6B, and IBM guides 2026 free cash flow up about $1B.

b10.evidence: Diluted EPS fell from $13.42 in 2015 to $11.17 in 2025 despite years of retained earnings and acquisitions, so retained capital has not clearly created matching value.

safety.evidence: A conservative DCF using IBM's ~4% revenue growth and ~20% FCF margin at a 12% discount rate gives roughly $125 a share after net debt, well below the $227.88 price.

fairprice.evidence: At about 18 times forward earnings and about 15.6 times trailing free cash flow with a 3.0% dividend yield, the price is reasonable for a mature business but not cheap for 4-5% revenue growth.

mu5.evidence: IBM's installed base and contracts make sudden failure unlikely, but AI-driven mainframe migration, hyperscaler competition, consulting deflation and $62B of debt are several plausible routes to slow erosion.

reinvest.evidence: IBM can reinvest in R&D ($8.3B in 2025) and quantum, but much of its growth comes from acquisitions such as HashiCorp and Confluent, whose returns are not yet proven.

ly2.evidence: IBM fits Lynch's stalwart category: a large, well-known company growing mid-single digits with a reliable dividend and a simple story of shifting toward software and AI.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 20.5 and forward P/E about 18.1, versus expected EPS growth of about 6-7% (consensus 2026 EPS $12.31, +6.3%), so the P/E is roughly three times the growth rate.

runway.evidence: Software, data streaming (Confluent), automation (HashiCorp), AI and quantum offer room to grow, but consensus sees only about 4% revenue growth in 2026 and 2027.

ly7.evidence: There were no open-market insider purchases (Krishna's February 2026 Form 4 shows only award vesting and tax withholding), and diluted shares rose from 896.6M in 2020 to 953.3M in Q2 2026 because buybacks have been suspended since the 2019 Red Hat deal.

ly8.evidence: IBM is covered by about 25 analysts and is one of the most widely followed technology stocks in the world.

fi2.evidence: IBM keeps renewing its product lines, launching the z17 mainframe in 2025, Telum II and Spyre AI chips, Granite AI models, the Lightwell security platform in July 2026 and a quantum roadmap to a fault-tolerant system by 2029.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $8.3B in 2025 produces strong mainframe and quantum hardware and many patents, but IBM's AI efforts (Watson, then watsonx) have trailed rivals commercially.

fi4.evidence: IBM's enterprise sales force and consulting arm give deep access to large clients, but in Q2 2026 many large deals did not close on time and Consulting revenue was flat.

longterm.evidence: IBM is committing more than $10B over five years to quantum computing and a $1B cash contribution to the Anderon quantum foundry, investments that will not pay off for years.

gr1.evidence: IBM had $67.5B of 2025 revenue, about $152B of assets and a market value of about $215B.

ni10.evidence: IBM reported positive net income in each of the last ten years, with the low point $1.64B in 2022 and $10.59B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: IBM has paid dividends every year for over a century and raised its quarterly dividend for the 31st consecutive year in April 2026, to $1.69.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS fell from $13.42 in 2015 to $11.17 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The $227.88 price is about 27 times average diluted EPS of the last three years ($8.14, $6.43 and $11.17).

gr7.evidence: With P/E about 20.5 and price/book about 6.3, the product is about 129, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Apart from mainframe reliability, IBM has no technology ten times better than rivals; its AI models and cloud offerings compete closely with Microsoft, Google, AWS and the AI labs.

timing.evidence: Enterprise AI adoption and hybrid-cloud demand favour IBM's software (up 11% in 2025), but the same AI wave threatens mainframe lock-in and consulting pricing, and quantum is still years from commercial scale.

th3.evidence: IBM is a mature incumbent spanning large established markets, not a company that dominated a small niche and is expanding outward.

team.evidence: Krishna, an engineer with a PhD from the University of Illinois, and CFO Jim Kavanaugh are seasoned operators who improved margins and cash flow, but they are not seen as a world-class team on the level of the top tech founders.

th5.evidence: IBM has direct relationships with most of the world's largest banks, insurers and governments in over 175 countries, plus a consulting arm that pulls through its software.

durable.evidence: Mainframe and core software positions have lasted 60 years, but AI coding tools that can modernise COBOL (behind the February 2026 sell-off) make durability over the next 10-20 years less certain.

th7.evidence: IBM's bet on a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029 and a dedicated quantum wafer foundry is a distinctive opportunity, though Google and others pursue the same goal.

trend.evidence: IBM benefits from enterprise AI (generative AI book of business above $12.5B by January 2026) and hybrid cloud, but it is a secondary beneficiary compared with hyperscalers and chipmakers.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth slowed from 9% in Q1 2026 to 1% in Q2 2026, full-year growth guidance was cut to 4-5% constant currency, and consensus 2026 EPS growth is only about 6%.

dr2.evidence: Confluent integration, Red Hat reaccelerating to 11% growth and Lightwell could improve results by 2028, but the Infrastructure downturn after the z17 peak and consulting weakness may persist.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would help IBM's $62B debt load and dividend appeal, but a slowing economy delays large consulting and infrastructure deals, as seen in Q2 2026.

dr6.evidence: Potential catalysts include Q3 2026 results, Confluent synergies, Lightwell adoption and quantum milestones toward 2029, none of them certain to move results sharply.

dr7.evidence: Slowing growth, guidance cuts, high debt and AI-disruption risk make IBM a poor candidate for a large, high-conviction position.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 58.2% in 2025, up from 54.0% in 2022, and the operating gross margin was 59.4% in Q2 2026.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow of about $13.8B on a market value of about $215B gives a free-cash-flow yield of about 6.4%, attractive for a stable business.

gb2.evidence: Trailing EBIT of about $12.8B against an enterprise value of about $270B is an earnings yield of about 4.7%, low by Magic Formula standards.

pa2.evidence: Q2 2026 weakness came partly from timing (post-z17 mainframe digestion and slipped deals), which is fixable, but the AI threat to legacy software and consulting may be structural.

pa4.evidence: Recurring software and mainframe revenue, $14.7B of free cash flow and a 31-year dividend-growth record limit downside, but $62B of debt and possible moat erosion leave some risk of permanent loss.

wo1.evidence: IBM is a recognised player in enterprise AI (watsonx, Granite) and a leader in quantum computing, but not a leader in AI models or infrastructure.

wo2.evidence: IBM's products are not on a steep cost-decline curve that opens big new demand; its pricing relies on premium, mission-critical positioning.

wo3.evidence: IBM combines AI, hybrid cloud and quantum computing efforts, but they are not yet converging into a fast-growing platform.

wo4.evidence: IBM's addressable markets in IT services, software and mainframes are large but growing modestly; only quantum could expand many times, and not within five years.

ac3.evidence: IBM is largely insulated from commodity prices, but about 60% of revenue is outside the US, exposing it to currency swings, and its $62B of debt and pension plans are sensitive to interest rates.

ns1.evidence: IBM's strategy prioritises margin expansion and pricing on mission-critical systems rather than passing scale savings back to customers.

ns4.evidence: IBM could be stronger in 10-20 years if quantum computing succeeds and Red Hat/Confluent keep growing, but its mainframe and consulting positions could weaken, so the outcome is not clearly better.

va2.evidence: IBM solves large, painful problems for regulated enterprises: running secure, always-on transaction systems and modernising decades of legacy code.

tn1.evidence: IBM sells into the AI and hybrid-cloud trend, but it is an old business retrofitting itself rather than a company built for that trend.

tn2.evidence: The market tends to see IBM as a legacy mainframe and consulting firm, while it is becoming a software-led company (44% of revenue) with a serious quantum effort, though the gap is widely discussed.

tn3.evidence: IBM is a large-cap US technology company, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew every year from 2020 to 2025 and IBM is profitable ($10.6B net income in 2025), passing two of three; it misses on cash versus debt ($8.1B vs $62.0B), partly explained by its financing arm's $13.0B of debt.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in each recent quarter (e.g. $2.2B in Q1 2026 and $2.5B in Q2 2026), but debt far exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 7.6% in 2025 and 1% in Q2 2026, with 2026 guidance of 4-5% at constant currency.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 4-8% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 20% gives roughly 25-28, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue rose 7.6% to $67.5B while total expense and other (income) fell to $28.97B from $29.75B.

tn9.evidence: IBM triggers instant kills: debt ($62.0B) exceeds cash ($8.1B) and trailing operating margin is about 18.5%, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: IBM faces no existential legal threat, but it carries routine litigation, export-control and government-contract risks, plus scrutiny of its large US federal consulting business.

tn11.evidence: IBM provides hybrid-cloud and AI software, mainframes and consulting that help large banks, governments and enterprises run secure mission-critical systems and modernise them, charging subscriptions, licences, hardware sales and consulting fees; clients choose it for reliability and trust.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (2.6%), institutional ownership 10 (66%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 5, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year 2020-2025 and free cash flow was positive and rose to $14.7B in 2025, but pre-tax margin did not expand every year (it fell to 1.9% in 2022 and 9.2% in 2024) and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 6.3x (2025), but assets excluding goodwill ($84.2B) are below total liabilities ($119.1B) and the current ratio was below 1 (0.96 at end-2025, 0.79 in June 2026); liabilities were 3.6x equity.

tn18.evidence: Krishna has improved margins and cash flow since 2020, but he has led for about six years, is not a founder and has made no open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: IBM beat consensus EPS in most recent quarters, but Q2 2026 revenue fell short (pre-announced in Krishna's July 14, 2026 letter) and full-year growth guidance was cut.

tn21.evidence: There is no co-CEO, no fraud suspicion and no auditor change (PwC), but IBM has made a string of large acquisitions (Apptio, HashiCorp, Confluent) and Q2 2026 gross margin declined 1.0 point.

tn22.evidence: IBM has $67.5B of revenue, $14.7B of free cash flow and does not sell shares to raise cash, so it avoids the hype trap.

tn24.evidence: With a free-cash-flow yield of about 6.4%, the price implies only low-single-digit growth, close to the 4-5% IBM guides for 2026, so expectations look modest but not clearly below delivery.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year average revenue growth of about 3.7%, an FCF margin of about 20%, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate, plus $8.1B cash minus $62.0B debt, the value is about $125 a share, well below $227.88.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 18.1 against EPS growth of about 6-7% gives a PEG of roughly 2.7, well above 1.
